phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar stop [t] followed by close front vowel [i]; the first syllable is light and leads into the long vowel.
Long open front vowel [aː] — the macron marks a reconstructed vowel length that Assyriologists infer from Akkadian phonology and cognates; the cuneiform signs do not encode length directly.
Bilabial nasal [m], open vowel [a], and voiceless alveolar stop [t]; the final -t is the feminine ending of Akkadian tiāmtu, 'sea'.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tee-AH-maht' — stress the long second syllable and let it open like a calm sea before the final consonants close it.

pronunciation.note: Tiāmat is Tier 1 because the macron on the first a marks a reconstructed vowel length — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. It is a pedagogical mark: a visible question that invites discussion about how the name was pronounced in Akkadian. Standard Assyriology writes Tiamat or Tiāmat; the Unicode form Tiāmat belongs to PuniCodex's phonological reconstruction hub.

domains.title: TIĀMAT — The Phonological Reconstruction Hub
domains.subtitle: Salt Water · Chaos Dragon · Cosmic Matrix
domains.lead:
The name is written 𒀭𒋾𒀀𒈲𒌈. Standard Assyriology transliterates it as Tiamat or Tiāmat, from Akkadian tiāmtu, 'sea'. But the length of the first vowel — the very mark that turns Tiamat into Tiāmat — remains a reconstruction, not a sign-given fact. It is here, in the space between the cuneiform sign and the spoken sound, that this temple operates. This node of PuniCodex is dedicated to the phonological reconstruction and didactic grammar of the ancient Near East. We mark vowel length not because it is certain, but because it is discussable. The macron is a question mark made visible.

Tiāmat is nevertheless the salt-water chaos mother of Babylonian cosmogony — the primordial sea whose mingling with Apsû's fresh abyss produces the gods, and whose defeated body becomes the sky and earth. She is the contradiction at the heart of creation: the mother who must be overcome for the world to exist.

mythology.lead: Tiāmat is the Babylonian primordial salt sea — the churning watery chaos from whom the gods are born and against whom order must be asserted. In the Enuma Elish she is first the generative mother of the divine generations, then the dragon-mother of monsters, and finally the cosmic body out of which Marduk fashions heaven and earth. She is not merely a sea; she is the possibility of both creation and destruction that precedes form.

myths.title: The Salt-Water Mother
myths.text: Before the gods existed there was no heaven and no earth, only Apsû, the freshwater abyss, and Tiāmat, the salt sea, 'their waters mingled as a single body' (Enuma Elish I.1–20). From their mingling the divine generations rose like silt from a river's meeting: first Lahmu and Lahamu, then Anshar and Kishar, then the sky-god Anu, and finally Ea, the wisest of all. Tiāmat is therefore the primordial matrix — the saline womb in which the cosmos gestates before anything has shape. Where Apsû is stillness, depth and the desire for quiet, Tiāmat is movement, breadth and the uncontained; when the younger gods are born, it is Apsû who wants them silenced and Tiāmat who refuses. The opening tablet means that creation begins as a marriage of waters, and that the mother of the gods is the one parent who did not want them dead.

myths.title: The War of the Gods
myths.text: When the younger gods' noise disturbed Apsû's rest, he resolved to destroy them — and Tiāmat alone said no (Enuma Elish I.44–59). Ea struck first: he cast the slumber-spell on Apsû, slew him, and built his own house upon the corpse of the abyss. But the victory turned the mother. Enraged and grieving, Tiāmat 'screamed aloud, furiously, day and night without ceasing' (II.89), and began the work of vengeance: she bred a monstrous army — serpents with venom for blood, dragons wearing haloes of flame, the bull-man, the scorpion-man, the storm-demons — and over them she set Kingu, her new consort, fastening on his breast the Tablet of Destinies (III.121–128). When the terrified gods could find no champion, Tiāmat had become what she had never been: not the womb of the gods but their executioner. The tablet means that chaos is not wickedness by nature — it is grief organized.

myths.title: Marduk Splits Tiāmat
myths.text: Marduk of Babylon accepted the challenge on one condition: that the assembly grant him supreme kingship, so that his word would bind the gods as Tiāmat's once had (Enuma Elish IV.3–26). Armed with the winds, the hurricane, the whirlwind and the seven winds, he rode out against her; when she opened her mouth to swallow him whole, Marduk loosed the evil wind to hold it open, drove in an arrow that pierced her heart, and 'extinguished her life' (IV.95–104). Then he stood upon the corpse and split it 'like a shellfish into two parts': half he raised up as the sky, half he laid down as the earth. The duel's meaning is doubled and uncomfortable. It is the charter of Babylon's empire — the city-god making cosmos out of chaos — and it is also the matricide at the root of the world: every ordered thing that exists, including the throne of Marduk, stands on the body of the mother.

myths.title: The Cosmos from Chaos
myths.text: Tiāmat's body became the inventory of the world. From her eyes Marduk made the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates; from her breasts he raised the mountains, boring springs in them to feed the rivers; from her tail he twisted the Durmāḫ, the 'great bond', to fasten heaven and earth together (V.51–66); her spit he made into the clouds, her foam into the winds and the thunderhead. Then he set the stars, the moon and the calendar in the sky-half, and assigned the gods their stations — the entire civilized cosmos laid out like an estate upon a corpse (Enuma Elish V). The tablet does not celebrate an annihilation; it records an ordering. The chaotic sea is not destroyed but reassembled — every city, mountain and river rests upon the body of the primordial salt-water mother. The myth means that chaos was not the enemy of creation but its material, and the world has never stopped being her body.

lore.syncretism:
Tiāmat's influence radiates across ancient Near Eastern and later mythologies.

The Unicode form Tiāmat is a reconstruction node: standard Assyriology writes Tiamat or Tiāmat, and the macron makes visible the open question of first-vowel length. In the Hebrew Bible, the primordial tĕhôm ('deep') of Genesis 1:2 likely preserves a memory of Tiāmat, now depersonified into the watery chaos that precedes God's ordering word. Greek sources knew the Babylonian chaos dragon through Berossus; later Jewish and Christian apocalyptic literature reimagined her as Leviathan, Rahab, and the great red dragon of Revelation. In modern fantasy, games, and occult cosmology, Tiamat survives as the five-headed dragon queen and as a symbol of primordial feminine chaos suppressed by patriarchal order.
lore.culturalLegacy:
The image of a cosmic sea-monster split to create the world has never lost its power.

It appears in biblical creation hymns that depict God dividing the sea and crushing Leviathan (Psalm 74, Psalm 89, Job 26), in medieval maps that place dragons at the edges of the known world, and in modern geology's recognition that Earth's water and land are products of ancient cataclysms. Tiamat has become an icon of feminist theology and eco-spirituality: the primordial mother whose defeat by a storm-god encodes the violence of order against nature. PuniCodex keeps the macron not as a settled fact but as an invitation: every visitor is welcome into the philological conversation about how this name — and the chaos it names — was pronounced.
lore.extendedMeditation: Tiāmat is the rare monster who is also a mother, and the myth never lets us forget it. Every generation of the gods is born from her mingling with Apsû; the cosmos itself is reassembled from her corpse. To call her 'chaos' and stop there is to read the victor's history: Marduk's triumph is a matricide, and the ordered world rests on the body of the parent who refused, at first, to let her children be killed. The myth asks its Babylonian hearers — and us — what order costs, and whose body pays for it. The restoration Tiāmat, with its visible macron, keeps the question alive at the level of the word itself: even her name, we confess, is a reconstruction; even the mother of everything must be approached through inference, humility and evidence.
lore.archaeology: Archaeological evidence for Tiāmat centers on cuneiform copies of the Enuma Elish from Nineveh, Sippar, Babylon, and Assur, where the myth of Marduk's defeat of Tiāmat was recited at the New Year (Akitu) festival. The Babylonian Esagila temple and its ziggurat Etemenanki embodied the cosmic order established by Marduk's victory. Representations of chaos dragons and composite monsters in glazed bricks, cylinder seals, and reliefs — notably from the Ishtar Gate at Babylon — give visual form to the creatures born from Tiāmat's body.
